title: The physician's sons (Kern ch. 15)
hookLine: a doctor's children take poison; he leaves word he's died so they'll take the medicine

cards: Nobody in the house will touch the bottle on the counter. It's the right medicine, and everybody knows it would help.
Still it sits there, because it smells strange, or tastes bitter, or because taking it would mean admitting something's wrong.
The Buddha promised a reason why he only seems to pass away, and he gives it the way the Lotus likes to: as a story. A doctor, a house full of children, a poison, and a medicine nobody touches.

teach.b: First, the poison. A wise and skilled physician has many sons. While he travels abroad, the children get into some poison and drink it.
When he comes home they're writhing on the floor, and they see him and cry out: father, you're back, help us. Second, the split. He mixes a medicine that looks, smells and tastes good.

Some sons, whose minds the poison hasn't reached, take it at once and are healed. The others are glad to see him and ask to be cured, but won't take it. The poison has turned their minds; the medicine seems wrong to them.
Third, the message. So the father makes a plan. I'm old, he tells them, my time is near.

teach.h: WORD COMES THAT HE HAS DIED.
teach.b: Then he goes away again and sends a messenger home with the news that their father has died. The sons are crushed.
If he were here, he'd look after us; now we're alone. And that grief brings them back to themselves.
They look at the medicine, see that it's good, take it, and are healed. When the father hears, he comes home, and they see him again. Fourth, the question.
Did that physician tell a lie? the Buddha asks. No, says the assembly. Neither do I, says the Buddha.
I seem to pass away so that people, missing me, will turn to the teaching I've left.
It's the same move as the burning house and the phantom city, and this time it's a father who wanted his children well more than he wanted them to see him.

how: In Mahayana communities that read the Lotus Sutra, the parable of the physician and his sons is told with the chapter on the Buddha's lifespan, to explain why the Buddha appears to pass away though he is always present.

o: brothers who learned medicine from their father abroad
children who took the cure only after their father seemed gone
sons who refused to forgive their father for leaving

games.q: take the medicine: tap the pairs.
p: goes abroad and sends word he's died
glad to see him, but won't take it

s: all the sons refuse the medicine at first
some, whose minds the poison hadn't reached, take it at once and are healed.
he sends word that he's died, then comes home once they've taken the medicine.
the Buddha asks whether the physician lied, and the answer is no
neither does the Buddha, he says, when he seems to pass away.

games.q: you're the physician. some of your children are poisoned, and they're glad you're home, but they won't take the medicine. what do you do?
o: hold them down and force it.
leave, and send word that you've died.
wait at home until they change their minds.
games.why: he goes away and sends word of his death. grief brings the sons to their senses; they take the medicine, and he comes home.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you know is good for you that keeps sitting on the counter: a hard conversation, an apology, a night of real sleep, a call you keep not making. Notice what makes it seem bitter, without arguing with it.
Then picture yourself picking it up and taking it, simply, the way the first sons did.

wordCard.voice: The physician's sons. Children who wouldn't take the cure until word came that their father was gone, and then they did. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: medicine, a remedy; the physician's gift to his sons.

carryVoice: Your line: take the medicine. It was good all along; only the poison made it seem wrong. Go gently.
